prompt: What is the difference between an application registration and a service principal?
hint: One says what the program is, the other where it acts.

choices.text: The registration is for people and the principal for programs
choices.why: Both are about a program; people are users.

choices.text: They are two names for the same object
choices.why: They are two objects, with two object ids.

choices.text: The registration defines it; the principal is its identity in one tenant
choices.why: Right. Roles go to the principal.

choices.text: The principal is the registration's secret
choices.why: A secret is a credential on the registration, not an object of its own.

prompt: A vendor's application is used by forty customer tenants. How many application objects and how many service principals exist?
hint: Count the vendor's own tenant too.

choices.text: Forty of each
choices.why: The registration exists once, in the home tenant.

choices.text: One application and one principal, shared
choices.why: Each tenant gets a principal of its own.

choices.text: Forty-one applications and no principal
choices.why: No tenant can use the program without a principal.

choices.text: One registration; 41 principals
choices.why: Right. The vendor's tenant has one too, beside the registration.

prompt: A script gives the Reader role to `shop-deploy` using its application (client) id as the principal. What does the lesson say about that?
hint: Which id names the object in this directory?

choices.text: Roles go to the service principal's object id
choices.why: Right. The client id is refused, or matches an unrelated object.

choices.text: It works, since the client id is the same everywhere
choices.why: Being the same everywhere is exactly why it names no object here.

choices.text: It works only for multitenant applications
choices.why: The audience has nothing to do with which id takes a role.

choices.text: It must use the registration's object id instead
choices.why: The registration is not what signs in; the principal is.

prompt: The portal lists service principals under *___ applications*.
Which `sign_in_audience` fits a tool only the shop's own staff use?

choices.text: `AzureADMultipleOrgs`
choices.why: That lets any work or school tenant in.

choices.text: `AzureADMyOrg`
choices.why: Right. This tenant only.

choices.text: `AzureADMyTenant`
choices.why: No such value: the provider refused it in the lab.

choices.text: `PersonalMicrosoftAccount`
choices.why: That is for personal accounts only, the opposite of staff.

prompt: In a new directory, `terraform init` downloaded `azuread` although it was in the plugin cache. A second `init` there took it from the cache. What made the difference?
hint: Which file did the first init write?

choices.text: The cache was filled only at the end of the first init
choices.why: Lesson 6 had already filled it.

choices.text: `rm -rf .terraform` cleared a stale download
choices.why: Removing it is what forced the second init to look again.

choices.text: The provider's signature expired between the two
choices.why: Both were the same signed file.

choices.text: The lock file the first init wrote
choices.why: Right. Terraform trusts the cache only for a directory that has `.terraform.lock.hcl`.

prompt: Which credential leaves nothing stored that could leak?

choices.text: A client secret with a short expiry
choices.why: It is still a string, stored somewhere until it expires.

choices.text: A certificate
choices.why: Its private key is stored, even if on one machine.

choices.text: A federated credential
choices.why: Right. It trusts another provider's token, and stores nothing.

choices.text: An access token
choices.why: That is what a credential buys, valid for about an hour.

prompt: The lab's token request answered `AADSTS700016`. What did Entra ID check before refusing?

choices.text: The secret, which it found to be wrong
choices.why: It never got that far.

choices.text: Only whether it could find the client id
choices.why: Right. With no application, there was no secret to compare.

choices.text: Whether the scope named a real API
choices.why: The refusal is about the application, not the scope.

choices.text: Whether the request came from a trusted network
choices.why: Network location is conditional access, lesson 11, and not what this code says.

prompt: What does `https://management.azure.com/.default` ask for, as a scope?
hint: Whose address is it, and what does `.default` mean?

choices.text: Resource Manager, with its existing roles
choices.why: Right. `.default` means whatever this principal was already given there.

choices.text: A token for Microsoft Graph
choices.why: Graph is `graph.microsoft.com`; this is Resource Manager.

choices.text: The default subscription's resources only
choices.why: Subscriptions do not appear in a scope.

choices.text: Owner of every subscription in the tenant
choices.why: A scope grants nothing; roles do.

prompt: Microsoft recommends a client secret's life be under how many months?
A team stores one client secret in five pipelines, with the maximum life the portal offers. What is the problem the lesson predicts?

choices.text: The portal will refuse the fifth copy
choices.why: Entra ID cannot see where a secret is copied.

choices.text: Five leak points, one shared expiry
choices.why: Right. Strings travel, and every secret expires one day.

choices.text: Secrets cannot be used outside Azure
choices.why: They work from anywhere, which is part of the danger.

choices.text: The secret becomes invalid after the first use
choices.why: A secret works until its date, as many times as it is sent.

prompt: Match each credential to what leaks if it leaks.

pairs.right: a string that is the program until it expires

prompt: In the GitHub exchange, what does the job send to Entra ID in place of a secret?

choices.text: Its GitHub password
choices.why: A job has no password; that is the point.

choices.text: A certificate stored in the repository
choices.why: Nothing is stored in the repository.

choices.text: The token GitHub issued to the job
choices.why: Right. Signed by GitHub, valid for minutes.

choices.text: The subscription id
choices.why: That is not a credential, and is no secret either.

prompt: The credential's subject is `repo:shop-example/storefront:ref:refs/heads/main`. A pull request from a fork runs the same workflow. What happens?

choices.text: It deploys, since the repository is the same
choices.why: Its token does not say `refs/heads/main`.

choices.text: GitHub refuses to issue a token to forks
choices.why: Whatever GitHub issues, Entra ID's comparison is what stops it here.

choices.text: It deploys to staging instead
choices.why: Nothing reroutes it; it gets no token at all.

choices.text: Entra ID refuses the exchange
choices.why: Right. Its subject does not match, so no token is returned.

prompt: Match each field of the federated credential to what it says.

pairs.right: who must have signed the token
who the token must be made for

right_distractors: how long the access token lasts

prompt: With federation in place, what is left that an attacker could use to deploy to production?
hint: Nothing stored can leak; what can still be changed?

choices.text: The permission to edit the registration's federated credentials
choices.why: Right. Whoever can widen the subject can let another branch in.

choices.text: GitHub's public keys
choices.why: Public keys verify; they cannot sign.

choices.text: The access token, kept in the repository
choices.why: It is never stored; it lives for one job.

choices.text: The client id, which is printed in the workflow
choices.why: It is not a secret; alone it obtains nothing.

prompt: Why does the shop add a credential with subject `repo:shop-example/storefront:environment:production`?
hint: What can a GitHub environment demand?

choices.text: Because branch subjects stop working after a year
choices.why: Subjects do not expire.

choices.text: To make production deploys wait for an approval
choices.why: Right. The job only starts once the approval is given.

choices.text: To give production a secret of its own
choices.why: Nothing about it is a secret.

choices.text: Because Entra ID accepts one subject per tenant
choices.why: A registration can carry several federated credentials.

prompt: Put the steps of the GitHub token exchange in order.
hint: GitHub speaks first and Resource Manager last.
items: GitHub issues the job a token for its repository and branch
the job sends that token and the client id to Entra ID
Entra ID compares issuer, subject and audience with the credential
Entra ID returns an access token
the job calls Resource Manager with it
trap: The comparison happens at Entra ID, not at GitHub: GitHub only says who the job is.

prompt: Which of these did the lab actually run for this lesson? Choose all that apply.
hint: Read the transcripts, not the steps.

choices.text: A token request that Entra ID refused
choices.why: Right: AADSTS700016.

choices.text: `terraform validate` refusing an audience that does not exist
choices.why: Right.

choices.text: Creating the service principal `shop-deploy`
choices.why: That needs Microsoft Graph and a sign-in.

choices.text: The token exchange with a GitHub job
choices.why: Not run: it needs a GitHub job and a real tenant.

choices.text: A second `terraform init` taken from the cache
choices.why: Right.

prompt: A partner company starts using the shop's reporting application. In whose tenant is the new service principal created, and who gives it roles?

choices.text: In the shop's tenant, by the shop
choices.why: The shop already has its own; the partner needs one in its directory.

choices.text: Nowhere: the partner signs in with the shop's principal
choices.why: A principal acts in its own tenant only.

choices.text: In both, kept in sync by Entra ID
choices.why: They are separate objects with separate roles.

choices.text: In the partner's, by its own admins
choices.why: Right. Each tenant gives roles to its own principal, and can delete it.
